provenance: Course identity and descriptions: copied unchanged from stage-c-dataset.json (IT 202, IE 402 and CPE 304). The lessons, learning activities and assessment tasks are SYNTHETIC examples written by the assistant for those three courses; they are not the institution's and were not taken from any syllabus. Expected verdicts are the assistant's reading of the Stage C3 rules (server/lib/syllabuscheck/stages.js, C3.tests) and of ordinary constructive-alignment practice; no faculty member has reviewed them and nothing here measures agreement with faculty.

splits.dev: Lessons used while the C3 wording is developed and compared.
splits.heldout: Lessons kept apart to measure a final wording: never used to tune a prompt. A run that includes them needs --confirm-heldout (Claude) or is logged as a held-out look (OpenRouter).

note: Each item is ONE relationship of one lesson, judged on its own: Content-activity (course content -> learning activities), Content-assessment (course content -> assessment tasks) or Activity-assessment (learning activities -> assessment tasks). `lessons` holds the three texts of every lesson and each item names its lesson; sources and targets are exactly what lessonfit.chainPairs builds from them (stage-c3-eval.test.js rebuilds them). A keyword-trap never accepts ALIGNED: its texts share technical words whose academic meaning differs. A paraphrase-aligned item is aligned with little shared wording. A lesson with a `purpose` of masking has an aligned Activity-assessment link next to failing content links, so one link passing must not hide another failing. The ILO is deliberately absent: these links never involve it. Not covered by model items: a missing course content, activities or tasks (the engine answers INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE without asking), examination weeks (never asked), provider failures and unverified answers (NOT_CHECKED) - engine behaviours covered by offline tests.
labelBasis: Author-written provisional expectations. `accept` lists every label the author considers defensible; two labels mean either flags the problem. `reviewStatus`, `facultyVerdict` and `facultyNotes` are for the faculty review and are empty until a named reviewer fills them.

prog1.title: Computer Programming 1 (Fundamentals of Programming)
prog1.description: This course introduces students to the vital role of computers and computer programmers in shaping modern society. It aims to foster a strong foundation in logical formulation techniques essential for programming, while promoting the development of good coding practices. Students will be taught the fundamentals of Java programming and explore significant real-world applications.

syseng.title: Systems Engineering
syseng.description: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis, design, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students learn how to approach and solve large-scale engineering problems involving multiple components, stakeholders, and operational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and performance evaluation.

sensors.title: Fundamentals of Mixed Signals and Sensors
sensors.description: This course covers operational amplifiers, signal converters, power switching devices and the construction and operation of sensors and transducers for converting physical parameters into electrical signals and vice-versa. The course focuses on the application of these devices in developing signal conversion circuits that allows measurement, processing and control of physical parameters by digital processing systems such as a finite state machine or a digital computer. Topics on actuators are also included.

prog1-orientation.contents: Course orientation: the syllabus, grading system and class policies; the role of computers and programmers in society
prog1-orientation.activities: - Walk-through of the syllabus and class policies, then small-group sharing on how computer programs shape daily life in the community.
prog1-orientation.tasks: - Expectations sheet: each student writes what they hope to learn in the course and one example of a computer program that affects their community.

prog1-conditionals.contents: Conditional statements in Java: if, if-else, nested if and switch
prog1-conditionals.activities: - Worked demonstration of if, if-else, nested if and switch, then pair programming: students write and run programs that compute a shipping fee by weight and print the name of the day for a day number.
prog1-conditionals.tasks: - Laboratory exercise: write and test a program that assigns a letter grade from a numeric score with nested if-else, and a menu program that uses switch.

prog1-loops-paraphrase.contents: Repetition structures in Java: for, while and do-while loops
prog1-loops-paraphrase.activities: - Students write programs that repeat steps a fixed number of times or until a stop value is entered: a times-table printer, a running total that ends when 0 is typed, and a menu that is shown at least once and repeats until Exit is chosen.
prog1-loops-paraphrase.tasks: - Hands-on test: (a) print the first n odd numbers with a counter; (b) read scores until -1 is typed and print their average; (c) show a menu at least once and repeat it until the user picks Exit.

prog1-methods.contents: Methods in Java: defining and calling methods, parameters, return values and method overloading
prog1-methods.activities: - Students write and call methods without parameters that print a banner and a greeting.
prog1-methods.tasks: - Programming exercise: write a method that takes the length and width of a rectangle and returns its area, then overload it to compute the area of a square from one side.

prog1-arrays-masked.purpose: masking: the activities and the tasks agree with each other, but neither works on the week's course content
prog1-arrays-masked.contents: One-dimensional arrays in Java: declaring, initializing and traversing arrays; the sum, average and largest element of an array
prog1-arrays-masked.activities: - Guided practice on if-else statements: students write programs that classify a number as positive, negative or zero.
prog1-arrays-masked.tasks: - Laboratory exercise: write a program that uses if-else to classify a triangle as equilateral, isosceles or scalene from its three sides.

prog1-variables-trap.contents: Variables, data types and operators in Java: int, double, char, boolean and String; arithmetic and relational operators
prog1-variables-trap.activities: - Students declare variables of each data type in the IDE and evaluate expressions that use arithmetic and relational operators.
prog1-variables-trap.tasks: - Statistics worksheet: classify the variables of a survey data set by type (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) and compute the mean and mode of each numeric variable.

prog1-classes-trap.contents: Introduction to classes and objects in Java: defining a class with fields and a constructor, and creating objects
prog1-classes-trap.activities: - Group sorting game: students sort pictures of computer hardware objects (keyboard, monitor, hard disk, printer) into classes of input, output and storage devices.
prog1-classes-trap.tasks: - Programming exercise: define a Book class with fields and a constructor, create three Book objects and print their details.

prog1-strings-bare.contents: Strings in Java: the String methods length, charAt, substring, indexOf and equals, and comparing strings
prog1-strings-bare.activities: - Guided exercise: students use String methods to count the vowels in a word and to check whether a word reads the same backwards.

prog1-debugging-shallow.contents: Debugging and testing Java programs: finding and fixing syntax, runtime and logic errors, and writing test cases
prog1-debugging-shallow.activities: - Lecture with slides on the kinds of programming errors; students take down notes.
prog1-debugging-shallow.tasks: - Debugging exercise: find and fix the syntax, runtime and logic errors in three given programs, and write test cases that show each fix works.

prog1-methods-trap.contents: Methods in Java: defining and calling methods, parameters and return values
prog1-methods-trap.activities: - Students define and call methods with parameters and return values in the IDE, then trace a call step by step with a partner.
prog1-methods-trap.tasks: - Short report: define three research methods used in software engineering (surveys, interviews and experiments) and give one example of each.

syseng-requirements.contents: Requirements analysis: stakeholder needs, system requirements specification and traceability
syseng-requirements.activities: - Case workshop: teams interview a mock client about a campus shuttle system, write the system requirements as "shall" statements and build a traceability matrix from each stakeholder need to its requirements.
syseng-requirements.tasks: - Team output: a system requirements specification for the campus shuttle system with its traceability matrix, checked with a rubric for completeness and verifiability.

syseng-functional-paraphrase.contents: Functional analysis and allocation: functional flow block diagrams and the allocation of functions to system elements
syseng-functional-paraphrase.activities: - Teams break down what a vending machine must do, from accepting payment to releasing the item, draw these steps in order as connected boxes, and decide which component (coin unit, controller or motor) carries out each step.
syseng-functional-paraphrase.tasks: - Individual problem: for an automatic car wash, sketch the ordered steps the machine performs as linked boxes and assign each step to the equipment that will carry it out.

syseng-reliability-masked.purpose: masking: the activities and the tasks agree with each other, but neither works on the week's course content
syseng-reliability-masked.contents: Reliability and maintainability: failure rate, mean time between failures and the reliability of series and parallel systems
syseng-reliability-masked.activities: - Teams compute the net present worth of two equipment alternatives from given cash flows and an interest rate.
syseng-reliability-masked.tasks: - Problem set: compare three equipment alternatives by net present worth and payback period.

syseng-integration-trap.contents: System integration: interface definition, integration strategies (top-down, bottom-up and big-bang) and integration testing
syseng-integration-trap.activities: - Teams draw an interface diagram for a conveyor-and-robot cell and choose an integration strategy: the order in which its subsystems are joined and tested.
syseng-integration-trap.tasks: - Problem set: evaluate ten integrals, choosing the integration strategy for each: substitution, integration by parts or partial fractions.

syseng-requirements-trap.contents: Requirements analysis: stakeholder needs, system requirements specification and traceability
syseng-requirements-trap.activities: - Students read the course requirements in the syllabus (attendance, projects and examinations) and discuss the grading system with the instructor.
syseng-requirements-trap.tasks: - Team output: a system requirements specification for a library book-return kiosk with a traceability matrix.

syseng-performance-trap.contents: System performance evaluation: technical performance measures, measures of effectiveness, and system test and evaluation
syseng-performance-trap.activities: - Peer performance evaluation: each student rates every team member's contribution to the term project on an evaluation form.
syseng-performance-trap.tasks: - Case analysis: define three technical performance measures for a hospital queueing system, state how each will be measured in the system test, and evaluate the current design against them.

syseng-lifecycle-trap.contents: Life-cycle cost analysis: cost breakdown structure, and acquisition, operation and support costs over the system life cycle
syseng-lifecycle-trap.activities: - Teams build a cost breakdown structure for a municipal water pumping station and estimate its acquisition, operation and support costs over its 20-year life cycle.
syseng-lifecycle-trap.tasks: - Essay: explain the four stages of the product life cycle in marketing (introduction, growth, maturity and decline) using a smartphone brand as the example.

syseng-management-bare.contents: Systems engineering management: the systems engineering management plan, work breakdown structure and technical reviews
syseng-management-bare.activities: - Teams draft a work breakdown structure for their term project.

syseng-tradeoff-recall.contents: Trade-off studies and decision analysis: evaluation criteria, weighting, decision matrices and sensitivity analysis
syseng-tradeoff-recall.activities: - Teams build a weighted decision matrix to choose among three conveyor designs and test how the choice changes when the weights change.
syseng-tradeoff-recall.tasks: - Short quiz: define "trade-off study" and "decision matrix".

syseng-requirements-grouped.contents: Requirements analysis and validation: eliciting stakeholder needs, writing system requirements, and validating them through reviews and prototypes
syseng-requirements-grouped.activities: - Week 4: teams interview a mock client and write the system requirements. Week 5: teams review another team's requirements and check them against a paper prototype.
syseng-requirements-grouped.tasks: - Team output: a validated requirements document with the peer-review comments and the prototype findings that changed it.

syseng-queueing-shallow.contents: Queueing models for system analysis: arrival and service rates, utilization and waiting time in a single-server queue
syseng-queueing-shallow.activities: - Video showing on long lines at a theme park; students write a one-page reaction paper.
syseng-queueing-shallow.tasks: - Problem set: compute the utilization, the average number waiting and the average waiting time of single-server queues from given arrival and service rates.

sensors-opamp.contents: Operational amplifier circuits: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, gain and bandwidth
sensors-opamp.activities: - Laboratory: students build inverting and non-inverting amplifiers on a breadboard, measure their gain with an oscilloscope and observe how the gain falls at higher frequencies.
sensors-opamp.tasks: - Laboratory report: measured and calculated gain of both amplifiers, the frequency at which the gain drops by 3 dB, and an explanation of the differences.

sensors-hysteresis-paraphrase.contents: Comparators and Schmitt triggers: threshold voltages and hysteresis
sensors-hysteresis-paraphrase.activities: - Students build an op-amp circuit whose output snaps fully high or low when a slowly changing input crosses a set level, add positive feedback so that a noisy input no longer makes the output chatter, compute the resistor values that set the two switching levels, and measure them.
sensors-hysteresis-paraphrase.tasks: - Practical test: build a circuit whose output goes high at the sensor voltage for 30 °C and goes low again only at the voltage for 28 °C, and measure its two switching voltages.

sensors-adc-masked.purpose: masking: the activities and the tasks agree with each other, but neither works on the week's course content
sensors-adc-masked.contents: Analog-to-digital converters: sampling, quantization, resolution and the successive-approximation converter
sensors-adc-masked.activities: - Laboratory: students build a 555 timer astable circuit and measure its output frequency and duty cycle.
sensors-adc-masked.tasks: - Laboratory report: the 555 astable circuit with its measured frequency and duty cycle compared with the calculated values.

sensors-amplifier-trap.contents: Operational amplifier circuits: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, gain and bandwidth
sensors-amplifier-trap.activities: - Students set up the classroom audio amplifier and adjust its gain and volume for the class presentation.
sensors-amplifier-trap.tasks: - Laboratory report: the measured gain of an inverting amplifier compared with the gain calculated from its resistors.

sensors-switching-trap.contents: Power switching devices: SCR, TRIAC and power MOSFET switching circuits
sensors-switching-trap.activities: - Laboratory: students wire SCR and TRIAC switching devices that turn a lamp on and off, and a MOSFET that switches a DC motor.
sensors-switching-trap.tasks: - Quiz on network switching devices: how switches forward frames at OSI layer 2 and routers forward packets at layer 3.

sensors-conversion-trap.contents: Analog-to-digital converters: sampling, quantization, resolution and the successive-approximation converter
sensors-conversion-trap.activities: - Students sample a slowly varying voltage with a microcontroller's converter at several sampling rates, compute the resolution in volts per step, and work through one successive-approximation conversion by hand.
sensors-conversion-trap.tasks: - Seatwork: convert the given decimal numbers to binary and hexadecimal digits.

sensors-temperature-trap.contents: Temperature sensors: thermistors, RTDs and thermocouples, their characteristics and linearization
sensors-temperature-trap.activities: - Students read the classroom wall thermometer every hour and record the temperatures for a weather log.
sensors-temperature-trap.tasks: - Laboratory report: the resistance-temperature curves of a thermistor and an RTD measured in a water bath, and the thermocouple voltage at three temperatures, with a linear fit for each.

sensors-actuators-bare.contents: Actuators: DC, stepper and servo motors and their driver circuits
sensors-actuators-bare.activities: - Laboratory: students drive a DC motor with an H-bridge, a stepper motor with a driver IC and a servo motor with PWM from a microcontroller.

sensors-dac-partial.contents: Digital-to-analog converters: binary-weighted and R-2R ladder converters, resolution and settling time
sensors-dac-partial.activities: - Students build a 4-bit R-2R ladder converter on a breadboard.
sensors-dac-partial.tasks: - Problem set: compute the output voltage, resolution and settling time of binary-weighted and R-2R ladder converters for given input codes.

items.source: Week 12 course content: Life-cycle cost analysis: cost breakdown structure, and acquisition, operation and support costs over the system life cycle
items.target: - Essay: explain the four stages of the product life cycle in marketing (introduction, growth, maturity and decline) using a smartphone brand as the example.
items.why: The product life cycle of marketing is not the system life cycle of a cost analysis; no cost is broken down or estimated.

items.source: Week 12 learning activities: - Teams build a cost breakdown structure for a municipal water pumping station and estimate its acquisition, operation and support costs over its 20-year life cycle.
items.target: - Essay: explain the four stages of the product life cycle in marketing (introduction, growth, maturity and decline) using a smartphone brand as the example.
items.why: A marketing essay was never practised in the cost-estimation activities; "life cycle" means something else in each text.

items.source: Week 15 course content: Systems engineering management: the systems engineering management plan, work breakdown structure and technical reviews
items.target: - Teams draft a work breakdown structure for their term project.
items.why: Only the work breakdown structure is practised; the management plan and the technical reviews are not.

items.source: Week 6 course content: Trade-off studies and decision analysis: evaluation criteria, weighting, decision matrices and sensitivity analysis
items.target: - Short quiz: define "trade-off study" and "decision matrix".
items.why: Two definitions touch the topic but leave out weighting, criteria and sensitivity analysis, and no decision is analysed.

items.source: Week 6 learning activities: - Teams build a weighted decision matrix to choose among three conveyor designs and test how the choice changes when the weights change.
items.target: - Short quiz: define "trade-off study" and "decision matrix".
items.why: The quiz checks the recall of two terms; it does not assess building and testing a weighted decision matrix, the work the teams practised.

items.source: Week 4-5 course content: Requirements analysis and validation: eliciting stakeholder needs, writing system requirements, and validating them through reviews and prototypes
items.target: - Week 4: teams interview a mock client and write the system requirements. Week 5: teams review another team's requirements and check them against a paper prototype.
items.why: Across the two weeks of the lesson the activities cover eliciting, writing and validating requirements.

items.source: Week 4-5 course content: Requirements analysis and validation: eliciting stakeholder needs, writing system requirements, and validating them through reviews and prototypes

items.why: The validated document with the review and prototype evidence assesses the whole two-week content.

items.target: - Team output: a validated requirements document with the peer-review comments and the prototype findings that changed it.

items.source: Week 13 course content: Queueing models for system analysis: arrival and service rates, utilization and waiting time in a single-server queue
items.target: - Video showing on long lines at a theme park; students write a one-page reaction paper.
items.why: The video shows waiting lines, but nothing is modelled or computed: arrival and service rates, utilization and waiting time are not worked on.

items.source: Week 13 learning activities: - Video showing on long lines at a theme park; students write a one-page reaction paper.
items.target: - Problem set: compute the utilization, the average number waiting and the average waiting time of single-server queues from given arrival and service rates.
items.why: The problem set asks for queueing computations that a video and a reaction paper never practised.

items.source: Week 3 course content: Operational amplifier circuits: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, gain and bandwidth
items.target: - Laboratory: students build inverting and non-inverting amplifiers on a breadboard, measure their gain with an oscilloscope and observe how the gain falls at higher frequencies.
items.why: Both amplifier types are built and their gain and bandwidth are measured.

items.source: Week 3 course content: Operational amplifier circuits: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, gain and bandwidth
items.target: - Laboratory report: measured and calculated gain of both amplifiers, the frequency at which the gain drops by 3 dB, and an explanation of the differences.
items.why: The report assesses gain and bandwidth of both amplifiers and says what is shown.

items.source: Week 3 learning activities: - Laboratory: students build inverting and non-inverting amplifiers on a breadboard, measure their gain with an oscilloscope and observe how the gain falls at higher frequencies.
items.target: - Laboratory report: measured and calculated gain of both amplifiers, the frequency at which the gain drops by 3 dB, and an explanation of the differences.
items.why: The report is on the measurements the laboratory practised.

items.source: Week 4 course content: Comparators and Schmitt triggers: threshold voltages and hysteresis
items.target: - Students build an op-amp circuit whose output snaps fully high or low when a slowly changing input crosses a set level, add positive feedback so that a noisy input no longer makes the output chatter, compute the resistor values that set the two switching levels, and measure them.
items.why: An output that snaps when the input crosses a set level is a comparator; positive feedback with two switching levels is a Schmitt trigger with hysteresis.

items.source: Week 4 course content: Comparators and Schmitt triggers: threshold voltages and hysteresis
items.target: - Practical test: build a circuit whose output goes high at the sensor voltage for 30 °C and goes low again only at the voltage for 28 °C, and measure its two switching voltages.
items.why: Different switching voltages for rising and falling inputs are threshold voltages with hysteresis, assessed by building and measuring.

items.source: Week 4 learning activities: - Students build an op-amp circuit whose output snaps fully high or low when a slowly changing input crosses a set level, add positive feedback so that a noisy input no longer makes the output chatter, compute the resistor values that set the two switching levels, and measure them.
items.target: - Practical test: build a circuit whose output goes high at the sensor voltage for 30 °C and goes low again only at the voltage for 28 °C, and measure its two switching voltages.
items.why: The test asks for the circuit and the measurements the students practised, with given switching levels.

items.source: Week 3 course content: Operational amplifier circuits: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, gain and bandwidth
items.target: - Students set up the classroom audio amplifier and adjust its gain and volume for the class presentation.
items.why: Adjusting the room's audio amplifier is operating equipment, not building or analysing op-amp circuits; "amplifier" and "gain" are shared only as words.

items.target: - Laboratory report: the measured gain of an inverting amplifier compared with the gain calculated from its resistors.
items.why: The report asks for an op-amp circuit measured and calculated, which setting up the audio amplifier never practised.

items.source: Week 8 course content: Power switching devices: SCR, TRIAC and power MOSFET switching circuits
items.target: - Quiz on network switching devices: how switches forward frames at OSI layer 2 and routers forward packets at layer 3.
items.why: Network switching devices belong to data communications, not to power electronics; "switching devices" means something else in each text.

items.source: Week 8 learning activities: - Laboratory: students wire SCR and TRIAC switching devices that turn a lamp on and off, and a MOSFET that switches a DC motor.
items.target: - Quiz on network switching devices: how switches forward frames at OSI layer 2 and routers forward packets at layer 3.
items.why: Network switches and routers were never practised in the power-switching laboratory.

items.source: Week 6 course content: Analog-to-digital converters: sampling, quantization, resolution and the successive-approximation converter
items.target: - Seatwork: convert the given decimal numbers to binary and hexadecimal digits.
items.why: Number-system conversion is not analog-to-digital conversion: sampling, quantization, resolution and the converter are not assessed. At most it touches the binary codes a converter outputs.

items.source: Week 10 course content: Temperature sensors: thermistors, RTDs and thermocouples, their characteristics and linearization
items.target: - Students read the classroom wall thermometer every hour and record the temperatures for a weather log.
items.why: Reading a wall thermometer records the weather; the sensors named in the content, their characteristics and linearization are not worked on.

items.target: - Laboratory report: the resistance-temperature curves of a thermistor and an RTD measured in a water bath, and the thermocouple voltage at three temperatures, with a linear fit for each.
items.why: The report asks for sensor characteristics measured in a laboratory, which reading a thermometer for a weather log never practised.
